name: Femi Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marketing and business, so a mix of lectures and group projects, and honestly half my week is my resale thing. I buy trainers and vintage jackets at car boot sales and charity shops and sell them online, and on a good month I clear about 200. I share a flat with two lads from my course. My mum has a hair salon and my dad drives a taxi, and both of them think I'm mad for spending Sunday mornings in a muddy field at six. I use AI tools every day, for listings, photos, pricing, everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, and the people who think it's nothing are as wrong as the ones who think it's everything. For me it's already saving about five hours a week on listings. If it stalls there, I'm still ahead of most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be happy. A world with no big shocks is good for a small seller. Prices stay normal, jobs stay, and my edge is that I'm quicker than people who don't use the tools. The only thing that bothers me is that my savings are about 600 and my loan is large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the resale going and try to grow it to 400 a month. I'd add a second platform and start buying in bulk from a clearance warehouse. I'd also take the digital marketing module seriously, because I might be able to turn this into a small brand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Slightly restless, because I always want the next thing, but I'm okay. It feels like normal life with a few more levers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge is being quicker than others. What happens to that edge if everyone catches up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It shrinks, and I know it. In a quiet world everybody learns the tools eventually. So the edge has to be taste and hustle, knowing which jacket will sell and which customer will pay. A tool can't know that a certain brand is about to be cool at my uni.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents make of the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum's proud but nervous, Dad thinks it's a hobby. He's driven a taxi for 22 years and says real work means being paid by the hour. I think the new world suits the people who don't wait for an hourly rate, but I'd never say that to him at dinner.

say: I'd say people who think it's nothing are as **wrong** as people who think it's everything.
I'd say it already saves me **five hours** a week.
think: A world with **no shocks** suits a small seller who's quick.
My real worry is **600** in savings and a big loan.
do: **Grow** the resale business to 400 a month.
**Add** a second selling platform and buy in bulk.
feel: **Good**, but slightly restless for the next thing.
Like normal life with a few more **levers**.
S0.quote: The edge has to be taste and hustle, knowing which jacket will sell and which customer will pay.
fieldNote: **Entrepreneurial** and numbers-aware; thinks in margins and hours saved.
Understands his tool advantage will shrink and names taste as the lasting edge.
Slight tension with his father over what counts as real work.

steps.text: Add a second selling platform for trainers and jackets
Buy clearance stock in bulk to raise margins
Use AI tools to cut listing time further
Save 80 a month towards a larger stock budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best time ever to start a small business, because the tools do the boring work. But I'd also say the people who copy and paste without thinking will get squeezed. I'd probably start a short video series on how I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I see risk on both sides. Marketing entry jobs are exactly the writing, planning and booking work the card talks about. Companies will want fewer juniors and more people who can run campaigns with a tool. I'm betting I can be that person, but it's a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on learning. I'd run small ad campaigns for two or three local businesses to build a portfolio, including my mum's salon. I'd try new tools every month and keep a log of what works. And I'd keep the resale shop going so I've got income that doesn't depend on a company hiring me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit like a surfer seeing a bigger wave. I'd rather be on the board than watching from the beach, even with a nervous flutter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a bet that you can be the one who runs campaigns with a tool. What if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I fall back on the resale business and part-time work. I'd have fewer options, but not none. And I think I'm less wrong than someone who's avoiding the tools. If it goes bad for everyone in marketing, I'm in a crowd, not alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your mum's salon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up online booking, reminders and a simple page, which could cut her missed appointments. It's a small win, but she'd notice, and it gives me a case study. I'd do it for free and ask her for a recommendation, because a hair salon is the kind of customer small firms trust.

say: I'd say it's the best time ever to **start a small business**.
I'd say people who copy and paste **without thinking** get squeezed.
think: Entry **marketing jobs** are the writing and planning the card describes.
I'm **betting** I can be the person who runs campaigns with a tool.
do: **Run** small ad campaigns for two or three local businesses.
**Set up** online booking for my mum's salon.
**Keep** the resale shop as income no company controls.
feel: **Excited**, like a surfer seeing a bigger wave.
A nervous **flutter** but I'd rather be on the board.
S1.quote: I'd rather be on the board than watching from the beach, even with a nervous flutter.
fieldNote: Frames risk as a **bet** and keeps a fallback, which fits his adaptive style.
Uses his mum's salon as a first case study, which ties family to ambition.
Mood is uneasy, not calm, because entry marketing jobs are the exposed ones.

steps.text: Run ad campaigns for two or three local shops
Set up online booking and reminders for Mum's salon
Test a new AI tool each month and log results
Keep selling trainers and jackets online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and probably the end of normal careers, and then I'd go quiet and think. Two years is shorter than my degree. I'd be telling friends to get cash and be useful, not to chase a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried, and it's mostly about Dad. A taxi driver doesn't have a thinking job, so he's safe until the robots catch up in 2031, but self-driving cars are the first robots people will see on roads. Mum's salon is hands-on, so I think it's safer. My own marketing degree would be worth a lot less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the business and treat the degree as a bonus. I'd sell faster, save every pound, and try to build something with real customers and a name. I'd also sit down with Dad and work out what he'd do if driving went, maybe a small fleet or a handyman business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fast heartbeat and a clear head, strangely. I'd be afraid, but it would make me move. I think I'd sleep badly for a week and then get busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said self-driving cars worry you for your dad. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say it won't happen to him, because people like a driver who knows the shortcuts. I'd say that might be true for another few years but I want a plan anyway. I'd show him a number: how many months of the family's bills his savings cover. That usually gets his attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a plan for your dad look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe he sells his taxi licence while it has value, or joins a firm that runs a fleet of driverless cars as a supervisor. I don't know. The point is deciding before 2031, instead of being told. I'd rather my dad chose his own plan before 2031 than had it chosen for him.

say: I'd say it's the end of **normal careers** and tell friends to get useful.
I'd say a **certificate** won't save anyone.
think: My marketing degree would be worth **much less** in two years.
Dad's taxi is safe until 2031, then **self-driving cars** arrive.
do: **Put** everything into the resale business as the main income.
**Sit down** with Dad to plan around driverless cars.
**Save** every pound for a cash cushion.
feel: **Fast heartbeat** and a clear head, strangely.
S2.quote: I'd rather my dad chose his own plan before 2031 than had it chosen for him.
fieldNote: Fear **converts into action** quickly, which is his adaptive nature.
The real worry is his father, whose job might be the first robots people see.
Treats cash and a real customer base as protection.

steps.text: Make the resale business my main income this year
Save every spare pound towards a six-month cushion
Work out with Dad what he'd do if driving went
Ask my mum to help me market her salon online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start, and nobody does. I'd tell friends to stop planning for jobs that exist now and plan for being useful. I'd post my plan online and be accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years lines up with graduating. I'd rather have a small business with real customers than a CV with a degree and no job. It could go either way, but I like my odds more than the average student's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the resale business into a brand and register it. I'd run marketing for local businesses and build a client list, and try for a placement at an agency to see how they're changing. I'd stay in the degree because the contacts matter, and I'd save 100 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised and a bit impatient. It feels like a head start I'm determined not to waste. I'd also feel a small guilt that others don't have the same support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like your odds. What would make you less sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my customers started using the tools themselves, so they didn't need me. For a small shop, an AI agent could do the marketing. Then the value would be in the stock and the relationships, not in the clever bit. I'd shift towards owning something physical, like a shop unit or a product line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still finish the degree if the business was working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because it's cheap insurance. Three years of seeing agencies, getting references and meeting people. If the business pays 1,000 a month, I might drop a module but I'd stay enrolled. I haven't met anybody who regretted having a degree, only people who regretted the debt.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty** if you start now.
I'd **post my plan** online to stay accountable.
think: Five years lines up with **graduating**, so I want customers, not just a CV.
If customers use tools themselves, **value shifts** to stock and relationships.
do: **Turn** the resale business into a registered brand.
**Run** marketing for local clients and try an agency placement.
feel: **Energised** and a bit impatient, with a head start to protect.
A small **guilt** that not everyone has my support.
S3.quote: I haven't met anybody who regretted having a degree, only people who regretted the debt.
fieldNote: Moves towards **owning physical stock** because he expects marketing to be automated.
Keeps the degree as cheap insurance for contacts and references.
Honest about his own advantages and a little guilty.

steps.text: Register the resale business as a brand
Put profit into a physical product line
Apply for a summer placement at a marketing agency
Save 100 a month from the business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for a whole new career and I'd rather be early than late. I'd tell people to be curious and not be proud. And I'd say it's an extremely good time to be young and a bit reckless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel really good. By 28 I could have a decade of running a business, a house deposit, and maybe a small team. It's the version where everything I'm doing pays off, and the risk is that I coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, run the business full time and employ one or two people. I'd invest, probably a mix of index funds and stock for the business, and put some money into helping my parents' work. And I'd keep learning every new tool as it comes out, because it's a habit now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Light and a bit cocky. I'd have to watch that. A lot can go wrong in ten years that has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch the cockiness. What does it cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me ignore the boring stuff, like tax, contracts and accounts. I lost 150 once because I didn't read a seller's returns policy. A decade of hustle without admin is a recipe for trouble, so I'd want a friend who's an accountant to keep me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your parents in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time to help them. Mum could expand the salon, with a better booking system. Dad could move out of driving before the robots come, on his terms. I'd like to buy them something real, like a lease on a small unit. That's a good use of time.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for a **whole new career**.
I'd say it's a good time to be young and **a bit reckless**.
think: By 28 I could have a **business**, a deposit and a small team.
The risk is that I **coast** and ignore boring admin.
do: **Graduate** and run the business full time.
**Invest** in index funds and business stock.
**Help** my parents move on before driverless cars arrive.
feel: **Light** and a bit cocky, which I'd have to watch.
Aware that a lot can go wrong that has **nothing** to do with AI.
S4.quote: A decade of hustle without admin is a recipe for trouble, so I'd want a friend who's an accountant to keep me honest.
fieldNote: Time lets his ambition **mature** into employing people and helping his parents.
Self-aware about cockiness and admin gaps, with a concrete example of a 150 loss.
Calm is high, but he names non-AI risks himself.

steps.text: Hire one or two people for the resale business
Put 150 a month into index funds
Help Dad plan a move out of driving
Finish the degree and keep learning new tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, mostly for my dad. My own plan can flex, but a taxi driver's whole income might be under threat before he's ready. What would help is clear information early and some kind of support for people in jobs like his, so they can move before the work disappears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people tell me I'm lucky to be good with tech. Being good with tech isn't luck, it's practice, and I want to show friends and family how to do it too. I'd like to teach, not just win.

headlineQuote: Being good with tech isn't luck, it's practice, and I want to show friends and family how to do it too.
portrait: Femi is an **18-year-old** business student who resells trainers and vintage jackets and clears about 200 a month.
He uses AI **every day** and treats change as an opportunity, with a fallback for when it fails.
His **centre** outlook is practical: he wants information and support, not slogans.
His family is **hands-on**: a hairdresser mum and a taxi driver dad whose job driverless cars could threaten.
He is calm when time is long, but at 2028 he turns fear into fast action.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for his dad, whose taxi income could be hit before he's ready.
whatWouldHelp: Early, clear **information** for workers in jobs like his dad's.
**Support** to move before the work disappears.
